 What Tennessee Residents Should Know About Open Enrollment Season
 By Currents - November 19, 2026 
 Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp 
 As November gets underway, many Tennessee residents have an important opportunity to review their health insurance coverage and prepare for the coming year. Open enrollment season allows individuals and families to evaluate their current plans, explore available alternatives, and make changes that could affect their healthcare expenses and access to medical services throughout 2027.
 Whether coverage is provided through an employer, Medicare, or the federal Health Insurance Marketplace, understanding enrollment deadlines and insurance terminology can make the process easier to navigate. For residents of Lakeland and communities throughout Shelby County, taking time to review available options can help prevent unexpected expenses, coverage gaps, and other complications when the new year begins.
 Understanding What Open Enrollment Means 
 Open enrollment is a designated period during which eligible individuals can enroll in health insurance, renew existing coverage, or switch to another available plan. Although the process varies depending on the type of insurance, the general purpose is to give consumers an opportunity to evaluate their healthcare needs and select coverage for the upcoming year. Outside these enrollment windows, individuals may have limited opportunities to make changes unless they experience certain qualifying life events.
 For 2027 coverage, the federal Health Insurance Marketplace open enrollment period began November 1, 2026, and continues through January 15, 2027. Tennessee residents who want Marketplace coverage beginning January 1 must select a plan by December 15, 2026. Those who enroll between December 16 and January 15 will generally have coverage beginning February 1, provided they pay their first premium by the required deadline. These dates are particularly important for individuals purchasing their own insurance rather than receiving coverage through an employer. [1] 
 Reviewing Employer-Sponsored Health Insurance 
 Many Tennessee residents receive health insurance through their employers. Companies typically establish their own annual open enrollment periods, often during the fall, although the exact dates can vary. During this time, eligible employees may be able to enroll in a different health insurance plan, add or remove eligible dependents, or make changes to other workplace benefits, including dental and vision coverage.
 Employees should carefully review any information provided by their human resources department or benefits administrator. Even when an employer offers the same insurance company as the previous year, premiums, deductibles, copayments, and covered services may change. Some employers automatically renew existing coverage, while others require employees to actively confirm their selections. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners encourages consumers to compare their available options and consider how changes in coverage could affect their healthcare needs and household expenses. [2] 
 Medicare Open Enrollment Has Different Deadlines 
 For older adults and other eligible individuals enrolled in Medicare, the annual open enrollment period follows a different schedule. Medicare Open Enrollment began October 15, 2026, and continues through December 7, 2026. During this period, beneficiaries can review their existing coverage and make certain changes to Medicare Advantage plans or Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage for the following year.
 Medicare plans can change their costs, covered medications, provider networks, and other benefits from one year to the next. Beneficiaries are encouraged to review their Annual Notice of Change and Evidence of Coverage documents to understand what may be different in 2027. Individuals who are satisfied with their current coverage may not need to make changes if their plan remains available, but reviewing the details can help identify potential differences before they take effect. Medicare provides plan comparison tools and enrollment information through its official website. [3] 
 Exploring Coverage Through the Health Insurance Marketplace 
 Tennessee uses the federally operated Health Insurance Marketplace, available through HealthCare.gov. The Marketplace allows eligible individuals and families to compare private health insurance plans, review available benefits, and determine whether they qualify for financial assistance. It is particularly relevant for people who are self-employed, work for employers that do not offer health insurance, or otherwise need to purchase individual coverage.
 Marketplace plans are organized into categories commonly referred to as Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Platinum, although the specific options available depend on the location and plan year. These categories generally describe how healthcare costs are divided between the insurer and the policyholder rather than the quality of medical care. Some households may qualify for premium tax credits that reduce monthly insurance payments, depending on their income and other eligibility factors. Tennessee residents should use updated household and income information when reviewing their 2027 options because financial assistance and available plans can change from year to year. [4] 
 Understanding Premiums, Deductibles, and Out-of-Pocket Costs 
 One of the most important parts of comparing health insurance plans is understanding how different expenses work together. A premium is the amount paid to maintain insurance coverage, typically every month. A deductible is the amount an individual must pay for certain covered healthcare services before the insurance plan begins sharing those costs. Copayments are fixed amounts charged for particular services, while coinsurance represents a percentage of covered medical expenses that the policyholder is responsible for paying.
 Another important consideration is the out-of-pocket maximum, which generally limits how much an individual must pay for covered, in-network services during a plan year. Once that limit is reached, the insurance company typically pays the full cost of covered in-network benefits for the remainder of the year. However, premiums, noncovered services, and certain out-of-network expenses generally do not count toward that limit. Understanding these distinctions can help households compare the overall financial responsibilities associated with different plans rather than focusing exclusively on monthly premiums. [5] 
 Checking Provider Networks and Prescription Coverage 
 Health insurance plans often maintain networks of participating doctors, hospitals, specialists, and other healthcare providers. Depending on the type of plan, receiving care outside the designated network may result in higher expenses or limited coverage. Residents who regularly visit particular physicians or medical facilities should review whether those providers participate in the plans they are considering. It is also useful to confirm network participation directly with healthcare offices, since provider directories may not always reflect recent changes.
 Prescription drug coverage is another important factor, particularly for individuals who take medications regularly. Insurance companies maintain lists of covered medications, commonly called formularies, which may organize prescriptions into different cost categories. A medication covered under one plan may have different copayments, coinsurance requirements, or restrictions under another. Reviewing formularies, preferred pharmacies, and any prior authorization requirements can help individuals better understand their potential prescription expenses before selecting coverage. [6] 
 What Happens If Someone Misses Open Enrollment? 
 Missing an open enrollment deadline can limit an individual’s ability to enroll in or change health insurance coverage until the next enrollment period. However, certain life events may qualify someone for a Special Enrollment Period. These events can include losing qualifying health coverage, getting married, having or adopting a child, or moving to a new location that meets applicable eligibility requirements.
 Special Enrollment Periods have their own rules and deadlines, so individuals experiencing a qualifying event should review their options promptly. Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program also operate differently from annual Marketplace enrollment, allowing eligible individuals to apply throughout the year. Tennessee residents can explore eligibility for TennCare and CoverKids, which provide coverage to qualifying populations under the state’s Medicaid and children’s health insurance programs. [7] 
 Taking Time to Review Coverage Before the New Year 
 Preparing for open enrollment does not necessarily require choosing an entirely different insurance plan. For some households, reviewing existing coverage may confirm that their current benefits continue to meet their needs. For others, changes in employment, household size, anticipated medical expenses, or prescription requirements may make it worthwhile to explore alternatives. Keeping a record of frequently used healthcare services, current medications, and expected medical appointments can make comparisons more manageable.
 Residents should also be cautious when receiving unsolicited calls, emails, or advertisements about health insurance. Consumers can reduce the risk of misleading information by using official enrollment websites, contacting their employer’s benefits department, or speaking with qualified insurance assistance professionals. The Tennessee Department of Commerce and Insurance encourages residents to begin reviewing their options early, understand enrollment deadlines, and carefully evaluate coverage before making decisions. [8] 
 Open enrollment season provides an opportunity for Tennessee households to consider how their health insurance coverage fits their financial circumstances and healthcare needs. While the available options and enrollment rules may differ, understanding important deadlines, reviewing plan details, and comparing potential expenses can help residents approach the process with greater confidence.
 With Medicare Open Enrollment ending December 7 and the next major Marketplace deadline arriving December 15, November is an appropriate time for residents to begin gathering information and evaluating their choices. Taking these steps before the deadlines can help individuals and families enter 2027 with a clearer understanding of their healthcare coverage.
